newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq insists its weapons disclosures complete.
newsitem.headline: Iraq insists its weapons disclosures complete.

text.p: Iraq said on Wednesday it was astonished a senior United Nations inspector had called its disclosures of past weapons programmes incomplete, maintaining it was in full compliance with UN arms resolutions.

Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed, former head of Iraq's Military Industrialization Commission, told the Iraqi News Agency (INA) Iraq had supplied "detailed, complete and comprehensive" reports on its weapons of mass destruction.
"The Iraqi side has received the (UN) statement with great surprise and astonishment," INA quoted Rasheed as saying.

Rasheed was responding to comments by Charles Duelfer, deputy chairman of the UN Special Commission (UNSCOM) charged under terms of the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire with ensuring Iraq did not have chemical, biological and ballistic arms.
Duelfer told Reuters on Tuesday "final" reports submitted by Iraq in August on all three weapons programmes contained "problems of error and omission".
Approval of the reports, known as Full, Final and Complete Disclosures (FFCDs), is a key requirement for lifting crippling sanctions imposed on Iraq after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

"The purpose of my visit was a message that the FFCDs as we see them have important problems," Duelfer said on Tuesday. "The initial assessment of our experts is there are important problems in each area."
Rasheed, who met Duelfer on Sunday and again on Wednesday, insisted his country had given a full account to the United Nations.
"What Duelfer said...about Iraq's announcements on its past weapons programmes contradict what he said in his meeting with us and lack objectivity," INA quoted Rasheed as saying.
"Rasheed said these announcements were detailed, complete and comprehensive, according to previous remarks by UNSCOM experts during tens of visits they undertook," INA said.

It quoted the minister as saying Duelfer, an American, was following U.S. policy "which aims to hinder the completion of the work of the (UN) Special Committee, which would then allow the Security Council to look into lifting sanctions on Iraq."
"Rasheed affirmed that the Iraqi side had carried out all its commitments required from the Special Committee under the related security council resolutions," INA said.
The row over Iraq's disclosures follows a series of stand offs in June and July when UNSCOM officials were denied access to inspection sites.
Iraq said its national security could be jeopardised by UNSCOM requests to inspect installations linked to presidential security or Iraq's elite Republican Guards.
Duelfer had been due to leave Baghdad on Wednesday, but UNSCOM staff said his departure had been delayed by one day for technical reasons.
UNSCOM head Rolf Ekeus is due to submit his six-monthly report to the UN Security Council on October 11 and visit Baghdad later in the month. He says he believes Iraq is still concealing banned arms.
INA said Iraq was confident the Security Council would not be swayed "despite all the US pressure exerted to impede it."
